summary: The 3GPP identified cases in which SIP private header extensions, the P- header fields defined in RFC 7315, need to appear in requests and responses where RFC 7315 does not allow them. This informational document updates RFC 7315 to allow that. It was replaced by RFC 9878.

eli5.summary: Some special labels on phone-call messages were not allowed in certain messages, but the phone standards group needed them. This relaxes the rule. It has since been replaced by RFC 9878.

questions: where can p-headers appear in sip
subtitle: Clarifies where SIP private headers may appear in phone call messages.

tldr.problem: RFC 7315 defined private header extensions for SIP used in 3GPP mobile networks, but had contradictions about where certain headers could appear. Real-world usage also required some headers in additional places.
tldr.mechanism: This informational update clarifies and expands the rules for where each P-header (P-Access-Network-Info, P-Charging-Vector, and others) may legally appear in SIP requests and responses.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can now correctly place these headers in messages for charging, location tracking, and network identification in 3GPP IMS systems. The document was superseded by RFC 9878.

today: RFC 7976 is an informational document that updates RFC 7315 regarding where private header extensions may appear in SIP messages. It was superseded by RFC 9878, which further updates SIP P-header usage.

sections.title: The Problem with RFC 7315
sections.content:
RFC 7315 defined P-header (private header) extensions for SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) used in 3GPP mobile networks. These headers carry information about the access network, charging, and visited networks. However, RFC 7315 had contradictions: statements in different sections said different things about where certain P-headers could appear, leaving implementations uncertain.

The document also had misalignments introduced when RFC 3455 was updated and replaced by RFC 7315. Additionally, the 3GPP standards group identified real-world cases where certain headers needed to appear in places RFC 7315 did not allow.
sections.eli5: The old rule book had confusing rules about where labels could go on phone messages. The message system needs to know exactly where each label is allowed.

sections.title: The Misalignments and New Use Cases
sections.content:
The misalignments involved several P-headers:

P-Associated-URI can appear in REGISTER 2xx responses (not plain REGISTER requests). P-Called-Party-ID can now appear in REFER method requests, and should not appear in responses. P-Visited-Network-ID cannot appear in NOTIFY, PRACK, INFO, and UPDATE methods.

The most significant new allowances come from 3GPP requirements. P-Access-Network-Info may contain Network Provided Location Information (NPLI) needed for charging and billing records in mobile networks. During session modification, the network may need location at the time of modification, which can be signaled via the ACK request. P-Charging-Vector carries operator identification information. In multi-operator scenarios, different transit operators may be selected for each SIP request direction, so this header must appear in ACK requests as well.
sections.eli5: One label goes in replies but not requests. Another label goes in a rare type of request. Two labels now go in acknowledgment messages too.

sections.title: Updated Rules for P-Headers
sections.content:
The updated rules from RFC 7315 Section 5.7 now state:

P-Associated-URI appears in REGISTER 2xx responses. P-Called-Party-ID appears in INVITE, OPTIONS, PUBLISH, REFER, SUBSCRIBE, and MESSAGE methods (removed from responses). P-Visited-Network-ID appears in all methods except ACK, BYE, CANCEL, NOTIFY, PRACK, INFO, and UPDATE (and not in responses).

P-Access-Network-Info appears in all methods and non-100 responses, except CANCEL, and ACK methods triggered only by 2xx responses. P-Charging-Vector appears in all methods and non-100 responses, except CANCEL and ACK methods triggered only by 2xx responses. P-Charging-Function-Addresses appears in all methods and non-100 responses, except CANCEL methods and ACK methods.

The key constraint: ACK methods triggered by non-2xx responses (errors) do not carry these headers, only ACK for successful responses.
sections.eli5: Each label has specific places it is allowed. The new rule lets location and charging information go in acknowledgments for successful calls, but not for failed calls.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
The security considerations defined in RFC 7315 still apply. These P-headers should only be sent to trusted entities within the same operator or trusted partners. The headers are assumed to be carried between trusted network elements, not across the public Internet.

This specification allows headers in places they were not previously allowed, but the same assumptions about trust apply. It also disallows headers in some places they were previously allowed, which could cause issues if older implementations have not been updated. The expansion of P-Access-Network-Info into ACK requests is particularly sensitive: this header may include privacy-sensitive location information. The security and privacy implications are the same as for P-Access-Network-Info in other SIP requests.
sections.eli5: These labels should only be used between phone systems that trust each other. Location information is sensitive and must be protected.
